newsitem.title: FRANCE: Foncier boss revives restructuring talks.
newsitem.headline: Foncier boss revives restructuring talks.

text.p: Credit Foncier de France chairman Jerome Meyssonnier said on Thursday he would start working again on a restructuring plan, in limbo since the government announced plans to break up the troubled home loans group in July.
Meyssonnier said in an interview in afternoon daily Le Monde he believed in the future of Foncier if it were "restructured, recapitalised and found a supporting partner".
Staff ended a sit-in at the bank's headquarters on Thursday after nearly three weeks, for several days of which Meyssonnier had been held "hostage" along with seven board members.
Meyssonnier told Le Monde that he had called a staff works committee meeting on Friday to kick off restructuring talks, which are sure to involve cuts in the 3,300 strong staff.
He reiterated, in a well-worn slogan of the past few weeks, that, "Whatever happens, Credit Foncier of tomorrow will be different from the one we know today".

The government announced plans in July for the cooperatively-run Credit Immobilier to take over the home loans portfolio of Credit Foncier and to spin off the rest into a state holding company for gradual wind-down.
The plan was announced after Foncier announced last April a 1995 loss of 10.8 billion francs ($1.9 billion).

But the government has now appointed a mediator to sort the problem out after running into fierce and well-argued opposition from unions and predictions by Meyssonnier himself that the group could make a profit of more than one billion francs for 1996.
"Talks on restructuring started in spring 1996 and came to a halt in July but will start again," he said.
As many as 900 staff had been in the firing line when talks on staff reductions, mainly through early retirement packages and non-replacement, were being drawn up.

Unions will now have to negotiate on two fronts, on one side trying to keep the government break-up plan on hold while they look for another solution and on the other, trying to reach agreement on a restructuring which is likely to depend at least to some extent on their efforts to keep the group intact.
